A.biggest_strength: Seamlessly integrates a clickable 32-element array with synchronized Python code execution, a live candidate funnel, and a dynamic scaling slider from n=1 to 1 billion with a visual halving ladder.
A.biggest_weakness: Does not discuss common implementation edge cases like duplicate element handling (lower vs upper bound) or integer overflow in static languages.
A.interaction_feedback: Everything worked smoothly and intuitively. Direct cell clicking in the array to set the search target is wonderful, Back and Reset buttons work flawlessly, the Python code highlighting accurately tracks execution flow, and the halving ladder in Section 2 makes the logarithmic scaling instantly clear. Keyboard navigation (ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, R) works reliably when the figure card is focused. Readers might only wish for an array input field to test their own custom array values.

Clicked 'Step' through all comparisons until target 83 was found at index 22.
Clicked 'Back' to verify backwards stepping through comparison history.
Clicked 'Reset' to return the search state to initial conditions.
Clicked 'Play' to test automatic stepping animation.
Clicked cell 6 (value 23) directly to test direct-manipulation target selection.
Stepped through comparisons for target 23 to verify mid selection and range updates.
Typed non-existent target 40 into the target number input.
Stepped through search for 40 until lo > hi, verifying not-found state, insertion index display, and code highlight.
Tested keyboard shortcuts (ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, R) on focused figure card.
Scrolled to Section 2 and tested log-scale array size slider at n=1,000 and n=1,000,000,000.
Inspected linear scan vs binary search comparison metrics and the full-scale halving ladder.
Tested mobile layout at 390 px width, checking 8-column wrapping of the 32 array cells and stacked layout.
Tested reduced motion mode (--reduced) to verify disabled transitions.
Tested dark theme mode (--theme dark) to verify color scheme and contrast.

B.biggest_strength: In-depth supplementary reference notes that thoroughly address real-world algorithm nuances (integer overflow, duplicates, lower bound, and half-open intervals).
B.biggest_weakness: Fragmented two-click-per-step interaction model, non-clickable array cells, and a severe text collision bug on mobile in Scene 4.
factual_errors: In Scene 4 at mobile width (390 px), the header text 'most compares for n sorted cells' and note '×1,000 cells: +10 compares' overlap directly into an unreadable tangle of characters.
In Scene 4, faint ghost text ('37 = 37' and pointer outlines) bleeds through behind the comparison bars due to incomplete hiding of the array elements.
B.interaction_feedback: The dual progression structure (5 scenes plus sub-steps) causes friction: stepping requires two clicks per comparison (one for mid compare, one for range drop), which makes walking through a search tedious. Clicking array cells does nothing, so the reader is restricted to the text field or three preset buttons. In Scene 3, an automatic timer loop kicks in and can fight manual stepping until paused. In Scene 4, the mobile layout suffers an obvious text overlap bug where two SVG text elements collide directly.

structured_output.reasons: Page A is clearly the better explainer for a programming blog post. It presents binary search with outstanding clarity and immediacy: a 32-element array where every cell is directly clickable, synchronized line-by-line Python code highlighting, a candidate funnel with mid pips, and a dedicated interactive log-scale slider from n=1 to 1 billion that dynamically renders the halving ladder to scale. Page B has commendable technical depth in its written notes, but its interactive figure suffers from a confusing dual-axis navigation model (scenes vs micro-steps), non-clickable array elements, and a broken mobile layout in Scene 4 where header and note text collide and overlap.
